title: What makes it feel expensive?
sub: A five-round game: pick the product card that feels more expensive, then see how strong the evidence behind each design rule really is.
description: What makes it feel expensive? An interactive Lab project by Riya Dutta testing five premium design conventions against the research behind them.
facts: Interactive experiment, live on the web
Five pairs of one product card, one change each
None collected; picks stay in the visitor’s browser

sections.title: Do premium design rules actually hold up?
sections.lead: Every designer knows the rules for making something look expensive: no discounts, lots of space, elegant type, round prices, no currency sign. I wanted to know how much of that is evidence and how much is habit.
paras: So I built a game. Each round shows the same made-up candle twice, changing one thing. You pick, then see the convention, the research behind it, and an honest rating of how strong that research is.

sections.title: And how strong the evidence is.

items.d: Fairly strong. Frequent price deals go with lower brand equity across brands (Yoo, Donthu & Lee, 2000), though it’s a link from a survey, not an experiment.
A learned code. White space means prestige because of its history in modernist design, and its meaning varies across cultures (Pracejus, Olsen & O’Guinn, 2006).
Real, but it depends. Typeface design shapes impressions along six dimensions (Henderson, Giese & Cote, 2004); there’s no single expensive font.
Mixed. Round prices “feel right” for emotional buys in five studies (Wadhwa & Zhang, 2015), but a 2018 replication didn’t clearly reproduce it.
Mixed. Diners spent about 8% more without dollar signs in one restaurant study (Yang, Kimes & Sessarego, 2009); the peer-reviewed version found no significant effect.

sections.title: Five rules, one with fairly strong support.
sections.note: “Looks expensive” is mostly a shared language: worth speaking fluently, and worth testing before you bet a launch on it.

sections.text: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so it loads instantly. Each round changes exactly one thing on the card, the left and right order is shuffled, and every claim links to its source. Nothing is tracked.
